messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rodrigo is a 54-year-old Latin American man, married and the owner of a mid-sized logistics company in the Houston metropolitan area. He came to the clinic after his wife issued what she described as an ultimatum: either he seek help, or she would no longer be able to remain in the marriage. His PCL-5 score of 69 places him in the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerged across the intake and first two sessions is one of a man who has been quietly drowning for years while working hard to appear in control.

Approximately three years ago, Rodrigo volunteered as a logistics coordinator for a humanitarian relief organization operating in a Central American conflict zone — work he had sought out partly from a sense of civic duty and partly, he admitted, because the challenge appealed to him. During his second month in the field, a convoy he was coordinating was ambushed. He was standing in close physical proximity to a colleague when that colleague was shot and killed. The sound of the gunshot was immediate and enormous, and in the seconds that followed Rodrigo found himself covered in blood, unable to move, certain that he was about to die. He was not physically injured, but he witnessed the deaths of two aid workers and was held at gunpoint for nearly forty minutes before the convoy was allowed to pass. He returned to the United States six weeks later.

In the months following his return, Rodrigo found that certain moments in his daily life had become unbridgeable passages back to the ambush. The crack of a car backfiring near his warehouse — where he spends most of his working day overseeing loading operations — would stop him cold, his body flooding with the same paralytic terror he had felt on that road. When employees or delivery drivers moved too close to him unexpectedly, brushing past him in a narrow corridor or approaching from behind, he would feel his chest seize and his vision narrow. More confusingly, and more distressingly, even moments of genuine happiness — laughing at dinner with his wife, feeling pride at a business milestone — would tip without warning into a kind of interior vertigo, as though the positive feeling itself were a signal that something terrible was about to happen. He had come to believe, without quite being able to articulate it, that feeling good was dangerous.

When these triggers fired, Rodrigo found himself reaching for strategies that offered some sense of relief or control, however temporary. He began carrying a concealed firearm everywhere — to his office, to restaurants, to family gatherings — telling himself it was a practical precaution, though he understood on some level it was the only thing that quieted the vigilance that hummed constantly beneath his surface. He would also, in the hours and days after a triggering moment, go over and over the ambush in his mind: asking himself why it had happened to him, what he had done wrong, whether he could have changed the outcome. He described this rumination as feeling like work — like if he thought hard enough, he would eventually arrive at an answer that would make the memory stop. And when the rumination grew unbearable, he would pick arguments with his wife, create friction with his business partners, manufacture small crises at the office — anything to fill the interior space with noise that was at least of his own making.

The tragedy of Rodrigo's coping is that it perpetuates precisely what it is meant to suppress. The arguments he engineers and the conflict he creates generate their own adrenaline, their own sudden sounds and physical confrontations, which re-activate the very triggers — the startle response, the hypervigilance to proximity, the confusion around strong emotion — that drove him to seek distraction in the first place. The weapon on his hip keeps him in a permanent state of threat-readiness, which ensures that every loud noise and every approaching body lands on a nervous system already primed to interpret them as lethal. The loop has been tightening for three years.

What finally brought him in was not the nightmares or the vigilance but a single moment: he had drawn his firearm in his own kitchen when his teenage son came downstairs unexpectedly in the dark. No one was hurt. But Rodrigo sat in the intake room and said, very quietly, that he was afraid of what he was becoming — and that he hoped, if nothing else, to become someone his family was not frightened of.
